claim: Since 2024-08-20 S3 supports conditional writes for PutObject and CompleteMultipartUpload: with the If-None-Match header the write fails if an object with the same key name already exists in the bucket, which prevents overwrites.
question: How can an S3 upload refuse to overwrite an existing object, and since when?

qualifiers.scope: general purpose buckets, PutObject and CompleteMultipartUpload

evidence.quote: | [Amazon S3 supports using conditional writes for `PutObject` and `CompleteMultipartUpload`](#WhatsNew) | You can check for the existence of an object in your bucket before creating it using a conditional write on upload operations. This can prevent overwrites of existing data. Conditional writes will validate there is no existing object with the same key name already in your bucket. For more information, see [Conditional requests](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-requests.html). | August 20, 2024 |
The `If-None-Match` header prevents overwrites of existing data by validating that there's not an object with the same key name already in your bucket.
If an identical key name is found in the bucket, the operation fails.

note: d072. Older material: S3 has no locking and the last writer wins; you had to build coordination in the application.

claim: On 2024-11-25 S3 added the If-Match header, which makes a write fail when the ETag you give does not match the object's ETag in S3, and the condition keys s3:if-match and s3:if-none-match, which let bucket policies force clients to use these headers.
question: What did S3 add in November 2024 for conditional writes, and how can a bucket owner require them?

values.spoken: the s3 if-match and if-none-match condition keys

evidence.quote: | [New HTTP header for conditional writes to check if the object has changed](#WhatsNew) | Amazon S3 adds the `If-Match` HTTP header to check an object's entity tag (ETag) before writing an object for some API operations. With this header, Amazon S3 compares the provided ETag value with the ETag value of the object in S3. If the ETag values don't match, the operation fails. For more information, see [How to prevent object overwrites with conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html). | November 25, 2024 |

| [New condition keys to enforce conditional writes](#WhatsNew) | Amazon S3 adds new condition keys `s3:if-match` and `s3:if-none-match` to use in bucket policies to force clients to use the `If-None-Match` or `If-Match` HTTP header. For more information, see [Enforce conditional writes on Amazon S3 buckets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes-enforce.html). | November 25, 2024 |

claim: On 2025-09-16 S3 added conditional deletes in general purpose buckets: a delete sent with the if-match header and an ETag succeeds only if the ETag matches the object, and the s3:if-match condition key in a bucket policy can require the header on DeleteObject and DeleteObjects requests.
question: How can S3 prevent a delete of an object that changed since you read it, and since when?

evidence.quote: | [Amazon S3 now supports conditional deletes in general purpose buckets](#WhatsNew) | Amazon S3 now supports conditional deletes in general purpose buckets. Conditional deletes verify that an object is unchanged before deleting it. Using conditional deletes helps you to prevent accidental deletions in high-concurrency, multiple-writer scenarios. You can now perform conditional deletes using the HTTP `if-match` header with an ETag value. Amazon S3 only allows your delete request to succeed if the Etag provided matches that of the object. Additionally, you can use the `s3:if-match` condition key in your S3 bucket policies to enforce conditional delete operations. For example, you can require clients to use the HTTP `if-match` header in both `DeleteObject` and `DeleteObjects` API operation requests, helping you to minimize the risk of accidentally deleting objects in your bucket. For more information, see [How to perform conditional deletes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-deletes.html). | September 16, 2025 |

CRC64NVME is now the default checksum algorithm; for uploads, all AWS-owned clients calculate a checksum and send it with the request, and S3 calculates its own checksum and validates it before storing the object.

evidence.quote: | [[New Amazon S3 checksum algorithm and improved checksum integrity features](AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity.html)](#WhatsNew) | Amazon S3 adds the `CRC-64NVME` checksum algorithm and improved checksum integrity features. The `CRC64NVME` checksum algorithm is the default checksum algorithm used for checksum calculations.
